newsitem.title: USA: Dollar weathers Yeltsin health rumors to end mostly flat.
newsitem.headline: Dollar weathers Yeltsin health rumors to end mostly flat.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed against major currencies Wednesday, despite a brief rally on market rumours of Russian President Boris Yeltin's death, dealers said.
The dollar made two pushes to shatter the ceiling of this week's narrow trading range against the mark, only to close slightly lower, at 1.5275 against Tuesday's close of 1.5295.

The dollar spiked on a mid-morning rumour that Yeltsin had died. The falsehood swirled through wary financial markets and briefly lifted the dollar and Swiss franc while hurting the mark, dealers said.
Dealers bought dollars and Swiss francs with the view that any ensuing chaos in Russia would have the least effect on the currency of those relatively stalwart and independent nations.
However, Russian authorities quickly denied the rumours, insisting that Yeltsin was working from a sanatorium outside of Moscow. The dollar quickly fell back to previous levels.
"It took a hold (of the market) for about 10 minutes," said Ben Strauss, trader at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
"The impact was very limited. I blinked and we were back to where we started," he added.
John Nelson, a dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank in New York, said such rumours typically have more impact in quiet trading days such as Wednesday's session.
Against the yen, the dollar stayed confined to a narrow trading range, closing slightly lower at 111.52 yen compared to 111.60 at Tuesday's close.
The denial of yet another rumour, which sparked a dollar rally against the yen in late U.S. trade on Tuesday, sent the dollar back down to its previous level, dealers said.

The director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, Eisuke Sakakibara, said on Wednesday rumours that U.S. officials had told him they could tolerate the dollar at an exchange rate of 120 yen were groundless.
If the rumour was true, it would have benefitted the dollar as such an informal agreement would pave the way for a strengthening of the dollar against the yen.
Also in early trade, a spate of institutional buying buoyed the dollar above critical levels versus the mark, but the move was short-lived and the dollar quickly shed its gains, dealers said.
Traders noted the dollar held relatively firm against the mark despite heavy investor buying of marks against other European currencies.

"It does still look like the dollar will continue to trade up," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole. He noted the dollar's rally last week to a 2-1/2 year high against the yen and 3-1/2 month peak against the mark.
Since then, the dollar has traded in a confined range well below those highs, dealers said.
Dealers look to U.S. economic data set to be released on Friday to give some impetus to the dollar.

However, others expressed doubt the U.S. September producer price and retail sales figures will affect the dollar given that the foreign exchange market virtually ignored a surprisingly weak U.S. September employment payrolls report last Friday.
"We've got some inflation figures at the end of the week which will obviously be a key piece of data, but we had some key data on Friday that didn't move the market higher," ABN-AMRO's Nelson said.
In other trade, the dollar dipped to 1.2532 Swiss francs from 1.2540 at Tuesday's close. Sterling edged higher to 1.5655 from 1.5635.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3532 from C$1.3539.
